messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 34
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Delivery Driver
  trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another
  pcl5: 46

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Negative Appraisals: Failed to Protect: I should have protected others and I failed, Inaction Guilt: I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened, Self-Blame: The event happened because of the way I acted

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Arjun Patel had been working as a delivery driver in a busy part of the city when the incident happened, on a late afternoon when traffic was thick and impatient and he was trying to stay on schedule. He had pulled his van into the curb lane near a small storefront, intending to drop off a package and get back on the road. In the moment that followed, he made a decision he has replayed countless times since: he moved the vehicle in a way he now believes he should not have, and someone was seriously injured. He has described the scene in fragments rather than a clean sequence, as though his mind returns to the sharpest points and leaves the rest blurred. What stays with him is the instant he realized the person was hurt, the helplessness of seeing the aftermath unfold, and the immediate, crushing thought that he should have protected others and failed. From then on, he came to believe that the event happened because of the way he acted, and he has not been able to let himself off the hook for not doing more to stop what happened.

In the weeks after the incident, Arjun tried to carry on with work because the family needed his paycheck and because sitting at home only gave him more time to think. But the ordinary demands of the job began to feel loaded with danger. He still had to drive through intersections, back into narrow spaces, wait beside moving traffic, and walk packages up to unfamiliar doors, and each of those moments could bring a sudden rush of the same shame and dread. The city streets around his route became saturated with reminders: a delivery address near the same kind of storefront, a horn sounding too suddenly, the sight of brake lights ahead, the feeling of maneuvering a vehicle in tight traffic. When he encountered these moments, he would tense, scan constantly, and feel pulled back to the afternoon of the injury as if it were happening again in his body. At times he found himself staring at the road but not taking in what was in front of him, while his thoughts returned to the belief that he had failed in the one moment when he should have been careful enough to keep everyone safe.

At home, Arjun became quieter and more withdrawn with his wife. He still went through the motions of eating dinner and answering questions, but he often seemed preoccupied, as though part of him was elsewhere replaying what he had done. When his wife asked how he was feeling, he would say he was fine or that he just needed to get on with it, but inside he was certain that he had done something unforgivable. He did not speak easily about the injury to the person he had harmed, yet he kept returning to the same self-condemning conclusion: he would never forgive himself for not doing more to stop what happened. This was not a passing regret for him but a fixed and punishing belief, one that seemed to settle over everything else. He would think about how he might have acted differently, how he might have seen more, moved sooner, or chosen better, and each replay ended the same way, with the sense that his action, and his inaction, had made the difference.

As the months passed, Arjun’s life narrowed around the effort to get through the workday without being overwhelmed by the reminders that seemed to wait for him on the route. He became more guarded on the road and more hesitant in situations that put him near traffic or tight spaces. The job that once felt straightforward now carried a constant sense of moral exposure, as though every turn of the wheel might confirm what he already feared about himself. That sense has also affected how he understands his place in his family. He watches his wife and thinks about the trust they place in him to provide and to be steady, and this only deepens his private conviction that he failed in a larger duty to protect others. Although he has not described elaborate rituals or dramatic outbursts, he has lived with a persistent inner accusation that leaves him tired, tense, and cut off from the ease he once had.

By the time he sought help, Arjun had reached a point where the burden of carrying the memory and his judgment of himself felt heavier than his efforts to ignore it. What brought him in was not a sudden crisis but the accumulation of months in which driving for work kept putting him face to face with the same triggers, and the shame remained unchanged. He is most afraid that he will never be able to see himself as anything other than the man who failed to protect others and did not do enough to stop what happened. At the same time, he is hoping, perhaps cautiously, that talking about it might make it possible to live without reliving that afternoon every time he gets behind the wheel.
